I am a 50-year-old man who has been farming these lands in Quzhou since I was young. I finished middle school, which is more than many of my neighbors, so I can read the seed labels and follow the county ag-station bulletins. My family has about 10 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, and I know every plot.

This year, I will stick with what works: **winter wheat followed by summer maize** on 8 mu of my best irrigated land. I thought about cotton because the price looked tempting last autumn, but I saw how many times the cotton growers had to spray—fifteen times or more—and how the bollworm always finds a way. That is too much labor and poison for a man my age. Vegetables pay well in the tunnel, but I do not have a tunnel, and the market price crashes when everyone harvests at the same time. Wheat and maize may not make me rich, but they feed my family, the state buys wheat at a stable minimum price, and I know the rhythm of these crops in my bones.

For wheat, I will buy an **improved variety** like Jimai 22 or Liangxing 99 from the seed shop in town. I never save my own wheat seed anymore; the shop-bought seed is clean, treated for disease, and yields better. I will rotary-till the fields after the autumn corn stalks are chopped and spread. Before sowing in early October, I will spread compound fertilizer as a basal dressing, and then top-dress with urea at green-up and jointing. The wheat needs three irrigations: one before winter to help it survive the cold, one at jointing in spring, and one at grain filling in May. I will spray herbicide once and fungicide/insecticide two or three times as the county station warns about aphids and rust.

After harvesting wheat in early June, there is no time to waste. I will **no-till sow maize** directly into the wheat stubble. Everyone around here does it now; it saves diesel, keeps moisture in the ground, and I can finish sowing in two days while the soil is still warm. For maize, I will buy **hybrid seed**, almost certainly Denghai 605 or something from the same company. The hybrids are expensive, but they give me 550 kg per mu or more if the weather holds. Maize needs less fuss than wheat—usually two irrigations, one at the V6 stage and one at tasseling, unless the summer rains are generous. I will spray herbicide once and maybe insecticide twice for corn borer.

My remaining 2 mu I will keep for the family vegetable garden and the courtyard; that is enough for our own eating and a little extra to sell at the village gate.
